summary:
Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.

The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.

In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. This federal policy is the framework a trans person in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under.
tangentialFactors:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights inside a single election cycle, and reversing it back. The 2020 policy protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion, the 2023 amendments restricted it, and the December 2024 decision restored it effective 1 January 2025. A visitor encountering school-facing rules in the province is reading a policy with a documented history of being rewritten by order of the executive rather than by statute.

The 2023 episode drew sustained public and political contestation. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, at which Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said the policy saves lives and warned that removing it would cost children. Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 consent rule.

Two provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans residents, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. Those rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they place New Brunswick's 2023 episode inside a wider provincial direction running alongside the human-rights statutes.

The national hate-crime climate cuts against the statutory protections. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the previous year; over the longer arc police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement. No New Brunswick-specific hate-crime figures are in the sources.

Informal use in the school environment requires no parental consent for a student of any age, with consent encouraged; entry of a chosen name into official records for a student under 16 still requires a parent's consent.

The policy binds school personnel, contract and casual employees, student teachers and volunteers as well as students, so staff in New Brunswick schools are directed to apply the name, pronoun and privacy rules rather than to adjudicate them.

Provincial correctional policy in New Brunswick is not documented in the sources: placement rules for provincial jails vary by province and no New Brunswick-specific rule is recorded. A resident held federally stands under the Correctional Service of Canada's 2022 gender-diversity policy.
